item.title: Russian diesel deal "a betrayal," bipartisan coalition says
item.description:
President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement.

Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine.

What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month.

  • While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans."
  • Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports.
  • However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea."

The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas).

  • The White House directed Axios to the president's remarks to reporters Tuesday.
  • He said described the agreement as a "diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market because the world market suffers with high prices. And when you knock out diesel refineries, that's not a great thing, but they're not releasing that to us. They're releasing it to the entire world."

Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal.

  • Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly."
  • Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition.

Friction point: As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington.

  • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin."
  • But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries, which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting that they halt such strikes.

What we're watching: The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions.

Go deeper: Trump's Russia deal leaves GOP candidates with a Putin problem

item.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
item.description:
The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure.

Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems.

  • "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios.

The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025.

  • These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services.

Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure.

  • Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications.
  • These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases.

Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services.

  • Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability.
  • Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services.

Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems.

The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems.

Go deeper: Shadow AI creates new headaches for company IT teams

item.title: White House pushes out Kimberly Guilfoyle after misconduct reports
item.description:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, announced her resignation Tuesday, shortly after the White House asked her to step down and following reports alleging misconduct before and during her diplomatic posting.

Why it matters: The exit of the president's longtime political ally and former fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. follows a series of Wall Street Journal reports alleging she used her political connections to seek financial favors and promote private business interests.

  • Guilfoyle has denied any wrongdoing.
  • White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday during her first press briefing that Guilfoyle was asked to resign.
  • "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said.

Driving the news: "My gratitude and respect for President Trump and Secretary Rubio remain unwavering," Guilfoyle wrote in a post on X on Tuesday.

  • "I am proud of what we accomplished together, and I will always be a loyal supporter of President Trump and his mission to Make America Great Again."
  • "While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end. It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America."

Guilfoyle's removal isn't entirely surprising, as Trump told reporters yesterday that he was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle following the allegations: "We're not happy," he said.

  • Those comments follow a senior U.S. official telling AP that Trump and Rubio were "extremely pissed off" about the reports and were considering dismissing her.
  • The U.S. Embassy in Athens and the State Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zacharia declined to answer additional questions about Guilfoyle and referred reporters to the president.

Catch up quick: The WSJ's Oct. 8 report said that Guilfoyle allegedly sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay a credit card bill before her Senate confirmation hearing and offered access to Trump administration officials in return. The donor did not make the payment.

  • An earlier investigation alleged she promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
  • The WSJ also reported that recordings captured Guilfoyle allegedly discussing private jet travel and luxury hospitality provided by wealthy Greek businessmen.

For the record: Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of messages the WSJ cited and the U.S. Embassy in Athens said she has followed State Department ethics and gift-reporting guidelines.

Zoom in: In her statement, Guilfoyle once again said that the allegations against her are "false."

  • "I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

Zoom out: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly defended Guilfoyle during a visit to Athens on Oct. 7, calling her "a strong ambassador."

  • A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations, saying he didn't know whether they were true.

Flashback: Trump nominated Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and California prosecutor, in December 2024. The Senate confirmed her in September 2025.

What we're watching: The State Department's inspector general is reviewing the allegations, AP reported, citing an unnamed U.S. official. It is unclear whether a formal investigation has begun.

  • Congressional Democrats have called for an investigation, with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, requesting on Oct. 10 that Guilfoyle testify under oath.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with more information.

item.title: Europe's alternative to Trump's China trade war
item.description:
Europe is testing a new response to China Shock 2.0, betting that it can confront Beijing's export juggernaut without resorting to President Trump's tariff-heavy approach.

Why it matters: More of the world is beginning to confront the threat that China's industrial overcapacity poses to their industries. But protecting individual sectors will not solve the bigger problem: China's factories are cranking out far more than its own economy can absorb.

Driving the news: The European Union and China struck a preliminary deal on Friday to sharply limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe.

  • The EU plans to initially cap Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports at 350,000 annually, potentially starting as early as December.
  • The cap would more than halve projected Chinese hybrid shipments, which were on track to reach roughly 800,000 this year, an EU official told reporters.
  • Imports totaled 302,000 in 2025. (Chinese officials Monday noted that the deal still allows its automakers to increase shipments from last year's levels.)
  • Vehicles exceeding the quota would be blocked rather than face additional tariffs.

The backdrop: France and Germany last week proposed giving Brussels sweeping new powers to restrict market access over unfair trade practices, a striking shift for Germany, which opposed EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024.

  • European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen warned in her annual address last month that the bloc's trade deficit with China had reached a "tipping point."
  • "Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," von der Leyen said.

What they're saying: EU leaders are considering tougher powers to confront Chinese trade practices, including one resembling the authority Washington has used to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods.

  • The agreement could dampen momentum for harsher measures, making member states "hesitant this week to rock the boat," Daniel Mullaney, an Atlantic Council senior fellow and former U.S. trade official, tells Axios.
  • Washington is pushing trading partners to join forces against China's industrial overcapacity.
  • "It's really hard for any one country to make progress on that if you don't have allies on your side," Mullaney says.

By the numbers: Chinese automakers ramped up hybrid shipments to Europe after the EU imposed steep tariffs on fully electric vehicles in 2024.

  • New data released yesterday shows that China's global passenger vehicle exports surged 64% in September, to 919,000, even as domestic sales fell 27%.

What to watch: Europe's deal could shift pressure to other industries — or perhaps even other nations — without addressing the underlying imbalances driving China's export boom.

  • Economist Michael Pettis argued over the weekend that the agreement would do little for European manufacturing overall.
  • "EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers," he wrote on X.

The bottom line: Europe's deal may provide breathing room for its automakers. But China's industrial might — and the pressure it is inflicting on manufacturers around the world — is not going away.

item.title: Five things to watch after Trump's Russian diesel deal
item.description:
President Trump is turning to Vladimir Putin to help ease a global diesel crunch, setting up a clash between Washington's energy priorities and its efforts to pressure Russia over its invasion of Ukraine.

Why it matters: The fuel shortage is among the most severe effects of the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.

  • Average U.S. diesel prices remain far above $6 per gallon, adding to GOP headwinds in the midterm elections. Trump says his deal will help bring costs down.

Catch up quick: Trump on Friday claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it.

A few things to watch...

The campaign trail. So far a few Republicans in close races — including Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan — have criticized the agreement.

  • Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes.

The market. Diesel futures dipped after the announcement. But analysts expressed doubt that the levels Trump is claiming will meaningfully sway prices in the U.S. and elsewhere — if Russia indeed delivers.

  • Per Trump's claim, Russia will "immediately" provide what amounts to 2.24 million barrels, followed 3.73 million next month (equivalent to around 124,000 barrels per day spread over a month), and then roughly double it thereafter.
  • "In the near-term, it's hard to see the waiver helping global fundamentals for diesel much," writes economics and geopolitics analyst Rachel Ziemba.
  • The global market currently has a deficit of about 1 million barrels per day, per market intel firm Kpler, and "Russia's ability to deliver additional barrels remains uncertain," writes Kpler's Michelle Brouhard.

Capitol Hill. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), one of those lawmakers in a close reelection fight, will try and force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases.

The law. It's not clear if any Russian barrels will reach U.S. shores — or whether it's legal if they do.

  • A bipartisan group of seven senators, in a statement, say the decision runs afoul of a 2022 law barring U.S. imports of Russian oil and petroleum products. Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence said it is acting "in compliance with all applicable laws."
  • Meanwhile, the White House faces an Oct. 18 deadline to begin implementing a more recent law — named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — that imposes fresh sanctions on Russia and trade penalties on buyers of Russian energy. But the law gives the White House discretion to waive key provisions.

Ukraine. Trump is pushing Ukraine and Russia to ease attacks on energy infrastructure.

  • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has criticized Trump's deal, said Russia has continued its barrages even as he maintained Ukraine held back early this week.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Axios-Ipsos poll: "Medicare for All" support surges
item.description:
Supporters of "Medicare for All" now outnumber opponents by nearly 2-to-1, according to a new survey of U.S. adults from the Axios-Ipsos American Health Index.

The big picture: Two-thirds of all survey respondents — and half of Republicans — said the federal government should be willing to spend more tax dollars to lower health care costs for Americans.

Why it matters: With three weeks to go before the midterm elections, and private health insurance premiums and prescription prices crushing voters, these findings suggest a path for swing-state candidates who embrace socialized medicine.

  • But the public's openness is driven more by desperation than by confidence in government. Affordability is foremost on most Americans' minds, and health care brings almost daily reminders of economic pressure.

Between the lines: Survey respondents say they want more government intervention — but they trust those leaders less than ever.

  • Trust in President Trump for health-related information fell to a survey low of 20%.
  • Trust in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fell to a survey low of 25%.
  • Trust in congressional Republicans (20%) and Democrats (25%) also were at lows.

By the numbers: 43% of Americans said they support the idea of establishing a "Medicare for All" program to provide government-run health insurance to all, largely replacing private health insurance; 24% oppose the idea and 32% say they aren't sure.

  • Nearly half of independents (47%) support it, as do 62% of Democrats.
  • 21% of Republicans support Medicare for All, and 27% are undecided, compared with 52% who oppose the idea.

The other side: Opponents said their top reason is they fear Medicare for All would have a worse quality of care than private insurance.

  • Other reasons were feeling it would become too expensive for taxpayers; that government should not be providing health care; or that it would expand the size of government too much.
  • But resistance to the idea has changed markedly from recent campaign cycles, when centrist Democrats were likelier to embrace a public health insurance option or a version of Medicare for All with a role for private insurance.

What we're watching: Respondents said they'd be more likely to support congressional candidates this year if those candidates favored expanding government subsidies of health care costs, reinstating enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired at the beginning of this year and expanding prescription drug discount platforms.

  • Republicans are less supportive than Democrats and independents. But the GOP is divided over expanding government subsidies for health care costs, with 31% more likely to back a candidate who supports the idea, 29% less likely and 31% saying it would make no difference.
  • Half of respondents said they'd be less likely to support a candidate backed by pharmaceutical and drug companies, compared with 7% saying they'd be more likely.

What they're saying: "Health care is one of the significant ways that people experience economic pressure every day," said Mallory Newall, Ipsos senior vice president for U.S. public affairs.

  • "'Medicare for All' is still something that many Americans have questions on" and "the amount of Americans answering 'not sure' tells me people's sentiments aren't fully formed," Newall said. Still, the current level of support is "noteworthy — and it is not solely driven by members of the Democratic Party," she added.
  • Depending on the candidate's party affiliation or the makeup of their district, "Maybe they don't call it 'Medicare for All,'" Newall said. But expanding federal programs to cover more Americans' health costs "is a message that can connect with voters during this cycle."

Methodology: This Axios-Ipsos Poll was conducted Sept. 25–28, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,122 general population adults age 18 or older.

  • The margin of sampling error is +/-3.0 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to correct Mallory Newall's title.
item.content:encoded:
Supporters of "Medicare for All" now outnumber opponents by nearly 2-to-1, according to a new survey of U.S. adults from the Axios-Ipsos American Health Index.

The big picture: Two-thirds of all survey respondents — and half of Republicans — said the federal government should be willing to spend more tax dollars to lower health care costs for Americans.

Why it matters: With three weeks to go before the midterm elections, and private health insurance premiums and prescription prices crushing voters, these findings suggest a path for swing-state candidates who embrace socialized medicine.

  • But the public's openness is driven more by desperation than by confidence in government. Affordability is foremost on most Americans' minds, and health care brings almost daily reminders of economic pressure.

Between the lines: Survey respondents say they want more government intervention — but they trust those leaders less than ever.

  • Trust in President Trump for health-related information fell to a survey low of 20%.
  • Trust in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fell to a survey low of 25%.
  • Trust in congressional Republicans (20%) and Democrats (25%) also were at lows.

By the numbers: 43% of Americans said they support the idea of establishing a "Medicare for All" program to provide government-run health insurance to all, largely replacing private health insurance; 24% oppose the idea and 32% say they aren't sure.

  • Nearly half of independents (47%) support it, as do 62% of Democrats.
  • 21% of Republicans support Medicare for All, and 27% are undecided, compared with 52% who oppose the idea.

The other side: Opponents said their top reason is they fear Medicare for All would have a worse quality of care than private insurance.

  • Other reasons were feeling it would become too expensive for taxpayers; that government should not be providing health care; or that it would expand the size of government too much.
  • But resistance to the idea has changed markedly from recent campaign cycles, when centrist Democrats were likelier to embrace a public health insurance option or a version of Medicare for All with a role for private insurance.

What we're watching: Respondents said they'd be more likely to support congressional candidates this year if those candidates favored expanding government subsidies of health care costs, reinstating enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired at the beginning of this year and expanding prescription drug discount platforms.

  • Republicans are less supportive than Democrats and independents. But the GOP is divided over expanding government subsidies for health care costs, with 31% more likely to back a candidate who supports the idea, 29% less likely and 31% saying it would make no difference.
  • Half of respondents said they'd be less likely to support a candidate backed by pharmaceutical and drug companies, compared with 7% saying they'd be more likely.

What they're saying: "Health care is one of the significant ways that people experience economic pressure every day," said Mallory Newall, Ipsos senior vice president for U.S. public affairs.

  • "'Medicare for All' is still something that many Americans have questions on" and "the amount of Americans answering 'not sure' tells me people's sentiments aren't fully formed," Newall said. Still, the current level of support is "noteworthy — and it is not solely driven by members of the Democratic Party," she added.
  • Depending on the candidate's party affiliation or the makeup of their district, "Maybe they don't call it 'Medicare for All,'" Newall said. But expanding federal programs to cover more Americans' health costs "is a message that can connect with voters during this cycle."

Methodology: This Axios-Ipsos Poll was conducted Sept. 25–28, 2026, by Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. This poll is based on a nationally representative probability sample of 1,122 general population adults age 18 or older.

  • The margin of sampling error is +/-3.0 percentage points at the 95% confidence level, for results based on the entire sample of adults.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to correct Mallory Newall's title.

item.title: A golden age of corporate profits
item.description:
Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax profit data includes inventory and capital depreciation adjustments.

Corporate America is raking in record profits, luxuriating in luscious margins and capturing the largest chunk of the country's income on record.

Why it matters: The corporate bonanza is bolstering the stock market, but it may also be playing a role in the persistently sour sentiment among the American electorate.

The latest: Tuesday is the unofficial start of third-quarter earnings season as JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and others report results.

Zoom in: Wall Street expects the members of the blue-chip S&P 500 index to continue to make it rain.

  • Third-quarter earnings per share are expected to grow roughly 29% for the index, compared with the quarter in 2025, according to estimate data collected by FactSet.
  • That's after a massive 50% annual increase in second-quarter earnings that was supercharged by the giant, non-operating gains on valuations of tech investments reported by Amazon and Alphabet. (Amazon, for example, penciled in its stake in Anthropic as boosting its profit by more than $50 billion.)
  • But even without those enormous gains, the numbers were quite strong, thanks to the AI boom that analysts expect to keep powering giant profits.

What they're saying: The market is still all about AI, but the gains are extremely concentrated.

  • "At the stock level, AI infrastructure stocks are expected to drive more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth in Q3," wrote Ben Snider, chief U.S. equity analyst with Goldman Sachs.
  • Snider noted that more than two-thirds of the total growth in S&P 500 earnings for the quarter is expected to come from just 10 stocks.
  • What's more, Micron Technology and Nvidia alone are expected to generate more than one-third of the growth in earnings for the blue chips, Snider wrote.

The big picture: Broader measures of U.S. corporate profitability captured by economic — rather than stock market — data also seem to show remarkable strength.

  • For the economy as a whole, after-tax corporate profits in Q2 jumped 18.2% compared with the same quarter of 2025.
  • And key measures of corporate profit margins across the entire U.S. economy are some of the fattest on record.
Data: FactSet, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax U.S. corporate profits, including inventory and capital consumption adjustments as a share of gross value added of U.S. corporate business. Reflects profits made within the U.S.; does not include profits produced overseas.

The other side: Boom times for corporate America have a flip side, however, with the so-called labor share of national income collapsing to some of the lowest levels on record.

  • The labor share tells you what percentage of the giant paycheck produced by the U.S. economy goes to workers in the form of wages and benefits, rather than to corporate profits, dividends, rents and interest paid to other economic actors, commonly summarized as "capital."

The bottom line: That decline helps explain the persistently sour mood of the American public toward the economy and its deep skepticism toward the AI boom that's producing this bonanza for American corporations.

item.title: Every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor as Microsoft reveals new Maia chip
item.description:
The trillion-dollar AI race is moving from software to silicon, as Microsoft's massive bet on its proprietary Maia chips proves Big Tech wants to wean itself off Nvidia's dominance.

Why it matters: Microsoft's plan to power its AI products with custom silicon shows how every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor, seeking lower costs, improved performance and more control.

  • The shift is particularly significant for inference — the computing needed to generate AI responses — as more sophisticated AI models and agents drive demand for computing power.

Driving the news: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its latest custom AI accelerator, saying it will begin deploying the chip in 2027 and it will become the primary inference system for its own products and services.

  • The company says Maia 300 will deliver 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.
  • It's also designed to minimize unnecessary data movement between chips and memory, a growing bottleneck as AI models become more complex.

The big picture: Microsoft's plan is part of a much broader shift, with nearly all major AI players seeking Nvidia alternatives.

  • Google has been developing its own Tensor Processing Units for years, with its latest generation including separate versions optimized for training AI models and running inference.
  • OpenAI is developing its Jalapeño chip with Broadcom, initially focusing on inference workloads. The company said in August that its first chip was outperforming Nvidia hardware on certain workloads and that it was already developing subsequent generations.
  • Amazon has its own ⁠Trainium family of AI chips, which are being used by customers including Anthropic. OpenAI has also committed to using Amazon's custom silicon as part of a massive infrastructure agreement.
  • Anthropic confirmed in August that it is exploring its own chip designs, even as it continues to rely on chips from Nvidia, Amazon and other suppliers.
  • Meta also has an internal chip development program, while continuing to buy substantial computing capacity from Nvidia and other suppliers.

Between the lines: Nvidia isn't necessarily losing business just because its customers are developing competing chips.

  • Nvidia's revenue more than doubled to $96 billion in the second quarter, a reminder that overall demand for AI computing leaves room for Nvidia chips and new offerings from Microsoft and others.
  • Like Microsoft, most Nvidia competitors are focused on inference, where margins are highest, while Nvidia remains dominant for training.
  • Still, Nvidia has begun to leverage its balance sheet to bankroll the AI buildout, so any competition that even slightly reduces its strength is noteworthy because it could weaken its centrality to continued growth.

What they're saying: Building competitive AI hardware requires designing entire systems, optimizing everything from memory and networking to software and power consumption, Rani Borkar, Microsoft's president of Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure, told Axios.

  • "We prioritize Maia for inference," Borkar said, describing it as the largest and fastest-growing opportunity for AI computing and an area where Microsoft can distinguish itself on cost and efficiency.
  • "For us, it's not an either-or strategy," she said. "We want a broad ecosystem while investing deeply in our first-party silicon."

Yes, but: Microsoft's plans to make Maia its primary inference platform apply specifically to Microsoft's own services, not necessarily to third-party Azure customers, including OpenAI.

  • Borkar also cautioned that the shift won't happen overnight. Maia 300 deployments will begin in 2027, but reaching multi-gigawatt scale will take time, extending beyond next year.

Reality check: As Axios ⁠previously reported, companies developing their own chips remain dependent on the same limited manufacturing capacity, advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory that Nvidia relies on.

  • That means even if custom chips can reduce dependence on Nvidia, they don't eliminate broader supply-chain constraints.

The bottom line: Nvidia remains central to the AI boom, but its biggest customers increasingly want to control more of the technology powering their own services — and capture more of the economic benefits for themselves.

item.title: Dems' red-state showings raise prospect of a bigger 2028 map
item.description:
Data: RealClearPolitics, American Presidency Project; Note: Nebraska's Senate race is between a Republican and an independent; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

Move over Wisconsin and Arizona. With Democrats making Republicans sweat in a host of red-state Senate races, a new batch of swing states may be emerging.

Why it matters: Some of the closest Senate races are in Nebraska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa and even Kansas. Sure, this could be a blip — or a reminder that it's a 50-50 moody nation, even in a bunch of red states.

  • The conditions that helped Barack Obama carry conservative states like Indiana and North Carolina in 2008 — an unpopular war, a bruising economy, an electorate hungry for change — could resonate again in 2028.

State of play: Democratic and Republican Senate candidates are running margin-of-error races in red states that not long ago were thought to be forbidding, or even a wasted effort, to many Democrats.

  • The Senate races in Kansas and Ohio are tied. So is Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn is trying to knock off Sen. Pete Ricketts.
  • Democrat James Talarico has consistently led polls in Texas, though that race appears to be tightening as money pours into the state on behalf of Republican Ken Paxton. Alaska is also a toss-up.
  • President Trump won all these states by double digits in 2024.

Zoom in: Republican operatives told Axios they're far from convinced that what's happening now will create a new slate of swing states in the 2028 race for the White House.

  • They see the current campaign as more of a one-off — a combination of dismay with Trump, high prices and uninspiring candidates.
  • "None of those states will be targeted [by Democrats] in the 2028 presidential. I will bet big money on that. But … all are in danger this year," one GOP consultant told Axios.
  • "It's a function of the atmosphere that we're playing defense in R+15 states. There's lethargy on our side," a Republican pollster said. "I don't think they're the new swing states per se."

But Democrats say better-than-expected performances by their candidates in several red states would at least open the door to an expanded map — with a big "if."

  • "An opening, yes," Obama's former chief strategist, David Axelrod, told Axios. "A guarantee, hardly."
  • Obama, he said, spent an enormous amount of time in rural communities and got to know voters. The Democrats who are faring well in those places this year have made a point of speaking with, not at, conservatives.

Yes, but: There's no certainty that Democrats will prevail in red states this year, much less set a path for 2028.

  • Polls are narrowing in several other Senate battlegrounds besides Texas, and the polling industry has had enough misses and challenges in recent elections to raise questions about whether we're getting an accurate picture of the political landscape at this time.
  • Either way, it's safe to say Democrats have made things interesting for the Nov. 3 election.

The big picture: The backlash against Trump has set the tone in many of these surprisingly competitive Senate surprise states, but Democrats also have also benefited from factors specific to each race.

  • In Ohio, former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is better known than the incumbent, Sen. Jon Husted (R).
  • In Texas, Democrats have a seminarian candidate in James Talarico who's emphasized the Bible's teachings as Republicans have tried to tag him as a radical leftist. His opponent, Ken Paxton, has been dogged by corruption allegations throughout the race.
  • In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton is the pastor of the largest United Methodist church in the country. His opponent, GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, has been hurt by reports that his former medical practice sued patients for even small unpaid bills, and that his 2020 campaign stiffed a bakery on a $700 bill.

What we're watching: To build on any openings Democrats might realize this year, the party will need a 2028 candidate who can appeal to center-right voters the way Democrats in red states have this year, Axelrod said.

  • "Part of the long-term problem for Democrats has been that it's still a party of working people, but it often approaches working people — especially in small towns in rural areas, in the spirit of missionaries and anthropologists," Axelrod said. Like, "we're here to help you become more like us."
  • So in 2028, he added,"it depends on who the candidate is, and what kind of bonds of trust that candidate can build."

item.title: Scoop: Top Trump operative enlisted to rescue Kansas senator's campaign
item.description:
A top Trump political operative has been tapped to help boost Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall's campaign in the weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the latest sign of how Republicans are scrambling to defend the red-state seat.

Why it matters: The hiring of veteran strategist Chris Grant reflects the GOP's growing anxiety over Kansas' Senate race. Marshall is running neck and neck with Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state President Trump won by 16 points in 2024.

  • Republicans fear losing Kansas could be a domino in costing them their Senate majority.

Driving the news: GOP operatives have become increasingly frustrated with Marshall's reelection campaign, which they believe hasn't been aggressive enough at a time when soaring fuel prices have particularly hurt farmers in Kansas and elsewhere in the Midwest.

  • Grant, who helped lead the main pro-Trump super PAC in 2024 and has remained involved in Trump's political operation, will be a senior adviser to Marshall and help guide strategy in the final three weeks.
  • Grant also worked on Marshall's 2020 Senate campaign.

What they're saying: "Chris is an absolute pro who has been a longtime friend to Team Marshall. Having him help land the plane these last three weeks is a no brainer," Brent Robertson, Marshall's chief of staff, told Axios.

Zoom in: Two GOP outside groups — the Senate Leadership Fund and Club for Growth — are pouring millions into the Kansas race.

  • SLF, the principal super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, is spending $14 million in Kansas after shifting resources from the Senate race in North Carolina, where Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper has a significant polling lead over former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley.
  • Trump said in a social media post Monday that he would campaign for Marshall "very soon."
  • A Democrat-aligned super PAC has announced plans to spend $5 million to help Hamilton.

Between the lines: Marshall has faced damaging headlines recently, including a New York Times report that his medical practice sued more than 700 former patients over unpaid medical bills, and that 81 were later arrested for missing court appearances.

The other side: Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, has won endorsements from two former Republican governors in Kansas, Mike Hayden and Bill Graves.

item.title: Feds search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in immigration probe
item.description:
Federal agents conducted a pre-dawn search Monday at the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) as part of an ongoing immigration probe, a DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios.

Why it matters: Searching Omar's home marks a substantial escalation of the Trump administration's fight with the outspoken progressive, who has condemned the immigration crackdown in her state.

  • It's also an unusual move against a candidate less than a month before an election, something the Justice Department has typically avoided.

The latest: President Trump said authorities are looking at Omar "very carefully" when asked whether he knew about the search of her home in advance.

  • "I've always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump said.
  • "I think she's a terrible person. She comes from a country that is a non-country."

What they're saying: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar said in a Monday afternoon post to X.

  • "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

Driving the news: Fox News first reported that Homeland Security Investigations agents conducted the search, citing a Justice Department statement.

  • A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios that DHS agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice" as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.
  • DHS referred Axios to the DOJ.

The other side: Omar's office blasted the search.

  • "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar spokesperson Jacklyn Rogers said in a statement.
  • "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."
  • House Democratic leaders separately issued a joint statement calling the search "deeply disturbing" and part of a "rogue abuse of power" by the administration.

Zoom out: Last month, border czar Tom Homan confirmed an ongoing criminal probe into Omar, though he declined to offer details.

  • Fox reported Monday that the search was tied to a fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork.
  • The Somali native came to the U.S. in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee.

Between the lines: Trump has for years demanded that Omar leave the country or be deported, citing, among other things, unsubstantiated claims that she married her brother to help him circumvent immigration laws.

  • Omar has dismissed the claims about the marriage in question as "baseless rumors."
  • Trump has made Minnesota's Somali community one of the most frequent targets of his anti-immigration rhetoric, and Omar the face of those attacks.
  • Just last week, he called on Minnesotans to "fight back" against the state's Somali population.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from President Trump, as well as statements from Omar, her House office and House Democratic leaders, and with more context.

Andrew Solender and Torey Van Oot contributed reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Federal agents conducted a pre-dawn search Monday at the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) as part of an ongoing immigration probe, a DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios.

Why it matters: Searching Omar's home marks a substantial escalation of the Trump administration's fight with the outspoken progressive, who has condemned the immigration crackdown in her state.

  • It's also an unusual move against a candidate less than a month before an election, something the Justice Department has typically avoided.

The latest: President Trump said authorities are looking at Omar "very carefully" when asked whether he knew about the search of her home in advance.

  • "I've always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump said.
  • "I think she's a terrible person. She comes from a country that is a non-country."

What they're saying: "I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar said in a Monday afternoon post to X.

  • "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

Driving the news: Fox News first reported that Homeland Security Investigations agents conducted the search, citing a Justice Department statement.

  • A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to Axios that DHS agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice" as part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.
  • DHS referred Axios to the DOJ.

The other side: Omar's office blasted the search.

  • "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies," Omar spokesperson Jacklyn Rogers said in a statement.
  • "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."
  • House Democratic leaders separately issued a joint statement calling the search "deeply disturbing" and part of a "rogue abuse of power" by the administration.

Zoom out: Last month, border czar Tom Homan confirmed an ongoing criminal probe into Omar, though he declined to offer details.

  • Fox reported Monday that the search was tied to a fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork.

  • Omar has dismissed the claims about the marriage in question as "baseless rumors."

  • Just last week, he called on Minnesotans to "fight back" against the state's Somali population.

item.title: U.K. prime minister attributes plot against U.S. bomber base to Iran
item.description:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the U.K. House of Commons Monday that Iran's Revolutionary Guard was "almost certainly" behind the suspected plot to attack the RAF Fairford base where U.S. bombers were stationed.

Why it matters: This was the first time the U.K. officially blamed Iran for the alleged planned attack.

What he's saying: "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by the IRGC. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said.

Driving the news: 10 days ago, the U.S. evacuated a dozen B-1 strategic bombers from RAF Fairford in response to intelligence indicating an Iranian drone attack.

  • It would have been an unprecedented and brazen move by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential to dramatically escalate the war in the Middle East.
  • The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base.
  • It was unclear whether the people who were arrested were connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack.
  • Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel provided the U.K. with intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack.

State of play: British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the Iranian ambassador was summoned to the foreign office in London to denounce the alleged Iranian plot.

The other side: The Iranian ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, told IRNA that Iran "categorically rejects" the allegations.

  • After his meeting with the UK minister for the Middle East, Stephen Doty, Mousavi said Iran had no involvement in the incident and asked the British government to provide evidence to support its claims.
  • He added that Iran is ready to cooperate with the British authorities in investigating the issue.

What they're saying: The U.S., U.K. and 27 other western countries published a joint statement on Monday condemning Iran for "use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."

  • The group said the threat against RAF Fairford "demonstrates the IRGC's continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors."

item.title: Trump's Russia deal leaves GOP candidates with a Putin problem
item.description:
Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise.

Why it matters: The agreement President Trump struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin Friday is designed to ease the cost of living for U.S. consumers. But Republicans who pleaded for help with fuel prices now face a fresh dispute over Russia, with energy analysts questioning whether the deal will deliver the relief Trump is promising.

The big picture: With three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are trying to answer voter anger while keeping up with a president whose proposed fixes keep becoming political liabilities of their own.

  • Trump's decision to lock arms with Putin adds another complication.

Driving the news: Weeks after signing a sweeping Russia sanctions law, Trump announced Friday that Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets.

  • The next day, Trump blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices and called for President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced, even as Russia continued attacking Ukrainian cities.
  • Republicans who just supported squeezing Moscow have three options in the final sprint for control of Congress: defend Trump's reversal, break with him or stay quiet.

Zoom out: The diesel deal packs some of the GOP's biggest liabilities into one decision: the Iran war's economic fallout, the party's split over Russia and a president determined to make the election about himself.

  • The deal also reverses Trump's own pressure campaign. Last year, he slapped an extra 25% tariff on India for buying Russian oil. On Oct. 2, he and other G7 leaders pledged to keep sanctions on Russia.
  • Energy analysts also doubt the deal will do much for diesel prices, which averaged $6.28 a gallon Oct. 11, up 71% from a year earlier.

What they're saying: The White House pushed back on criticism of Trump's record: "President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said.

  • A senior administration official said Trump is "laser-focused on bringing down costs, whether it's diesel with the Russians or importing Argentine beef. Some people might not like it, but he's thinking of what Americans are paying and what he can do about it."

Friction point: The internal pushback has been swift.

  • Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed to force a House vote blocking the oil purchases.
  • Reps. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) and Michael McCaul (R-Texas), along with Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and John Curtis (R-Utah), already criticized the deal by Sunday.
  • Tillis told NBC News' "Meet the Press" that Trump's deal may violate a law that requires the White House to notify Congress before lifting sanctions.
  • Even MAGA ally Laura Loomer denounced the deal as not only funding Russia but indirectly helping Iran by putting "money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran."

Yes, but: Some Republicans, like Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (Fla.) and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, backed the deal.

How we got here: Farm-state Republicans have pleaded with the White House to deliver diesel relief.

  • Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and others urged Trump to ban diesel exports, something the president embraced before the White House abruptly reversed and ruled out a ban.
  • GOP candidates in key Senate races, like Iowa's Ashley Hinson and Michigan's Mike Rogers, have called for ending the Iran war after previously supporting it. Instead, Trump has defended it in vivid terms, saying Iran might have attacked Los Angeles and San Diego if not for his war.

Between the lines: Trump's unpopular positions collide with voter sentiment as he touts the war with Iran, the rise of data centers and his own popularity.

  • His efforts to give Republicans something to campaign on leave candidates exposed through big promises, about-faces and proposals that won't materialize before voters cast their ballots.

Data centers: Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) has faced Democratic attacks over data centers, an issue the National Republican Senatorial Committee has identified as a vulnerability. Yet Trump used a Husted rally last week to defend the projects: "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China."

Dividend checks: Voters have also rejected Trump's proposed $5,000 dividend checks that analysts say would cost $1.3 trillion. A September Reuters/Ipsos poll found 63% of Americans disapproved.

Trump: Trump has insisted the midterms should be a referendum on his presidency, telling Republicans at last month's convention to "pretend that I'm on the ballot."

  • But a Pew Research Centerpoll released Thursday found 44% of registered voters view their congressional vote as a vote against Trump, compared with 19% who see it as a vote for him.
  • Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed oil prices, the Iran war and the midterm convention for falling poll numbers.

The bottom line: For Republican candidates, the challenge isn't just selling Trump's record. It's keeping up with a president who continues to give them new decisions to defend.

item.title: Business faces a more interventionist Washington post-midterms
item.description:
Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from Tuesday if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms.

The new analysis by FGS, a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections.

  • FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty.
  • "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says.

Zoom in: Michael Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness."

  • "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality."
  • "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman added. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty."
Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images

Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns.

  1. "Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business."
  2. "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue."
  3. "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style."

The bottom line: "Divided government does not necessarily mean lower political/legislative risk," FGS writes. "It may mean that policy/political conflict moves in less predictable ways."

  • Get the 16-page FGS report.

item.title: Trump privately expresses doubts about livestreaming execution
item.description:
President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of a former Army major who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas, according to four people who have spoken with the president.

Why it matters: Trump has been deluged with "negative input" about the idea from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers as well as advisers inside and outside of his White House, a senior administration official said.

  • A livestream of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen," Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios.
  • "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think."

Zoom in: Hasan faces a firing squad at Fort Hood, where he went on his murderous shooting rampage 17 years ago. He would be the first person in the U.S. whose execution would be livestreamed.

  • Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the norm-shattering idea Thursday on Real America's Voice.
  • "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it — that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

Zoom out: The idea was roundly condemned domestically and internationally. In the ensuing days, Trump started to publicly shift his positions:

  • At first, Trump was full-throated in his support. "Absolutely, I approve," Trump told reporters early Friday evening.
  • Later that night, Trump was more nuanced: "They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision."
  • On Saturday, Trump took control by telling reporters he would have the final say: "There are two thoughts: Don't show it and show it. 'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we'll make a decision," the president told reporters at the White House.

Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance has signaled where he thinks the president is going with the decision, according to a source.

  • "I don't know if that's actually going to happen," Vance, speaking off the cuff, told reporters Friday. He has privately repeated that to others.
  • "I'm not going to be watching it," Vance said.

Between the lines: Trump, Vance and everyone else in the administration is clear about supporting Hasan's execution. But the president is grappling with competing pressures.

  • "The president wants the bastard to pay, and a public execution might be that extra humiliation [Hasan] deserves," another confidant who spoke with the president said. "At the same time, he doesn't want to make the guy a martyr."
  • Said another: "This is an old dude in a wheelchair we're shooting. We want to livestream that?" (Hasan, 56, was permanently injured when he was shot during his capture.)

Friction point: The divide in opinion over livestreaming the execution is another point of disagreement between Vance and Hegseth.

  • They've been on opposite sides when it comes to the use of military force in Yemen and Iran, to the leadership of the Army.
  • Advisers say the men have a good relationship.

Context: Whether at the state or federal level, executions often are witnessed only by family members or select media. They haven't been livestreamed.

  • Executions used to be viewed in public squares, but that practice was discontinued in the 1930s, according to NPR.
  • Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh's 2001 execution was viewable to loved ones and bombing survivors via a private closed-circuit telecast.

Flashback: Yelling "Allahu Akbar!" Hasan fatally shot 13 people — including a pregnant woman — and wounded 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, when they lined up for medical checks at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center.

  • The rampage was the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11.
  • A special Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee report criticized the military for "political correctness" that blinded authorities to the major's increasingly clear Islamist radicalization.

The bottom line: Hasan will be executed unless something unexpected happens. The only real doubt is whether private citizens with no attachment to the case will be able to witness it.

  • "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this," said one administration official. "But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do."
  • "Hasan will be executed for his crimes," the official said, "and that's what matters."

The bottom line: Hasan will be executed unless something unexpected happens. The only real doubt is whether private citizens with no attachment to the case will be able to witness it.

  • "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this," said one administration official. "But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do."
  • "Hasan will be executed for his crimes," the official said, "and that's what matters."

item.title: Two U.S. professors win Nobel prize in economics
item.description:
Stanford University's Robert E. Hall and Columbia University's Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for research on how policymakers can stabilize economies, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday.

Why it matters: Their work helped shape how central banks set interest rates and communicate policy. The win comes as those institutions fight energy-driven inflation and risks to economic growth.

Zoom out: For decades, policymakers relied on economic models that linked higher inflation with lower unemployment. But that framework broke down during the 1970s stagflation when both prices and joblessness surged at the same time.

  • "The solution by Robert Hall and Michael Woodford was to build a new framework ground up," Timo Boppart, a member of the Nobel economics prize committee, said on Monday.

What they're saying: Woodford, who called into Monday's press conference hosted by the committee, said he was "elated" by the win.

  • "It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise — but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford said.

The intrigue: Asked by a reporter about the threat to the global economy, Woodford said the Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets and driven price changes with consequences far beyond the region.

  • He pointed to the 2008 financial crisis as a key test of his research, when central banks cut interest rates to near zero but struggled to revive economic activity.
  • His framework helped explain how other tools, including forward guidance and asset purchases, could support the economy.

Zoom in: In research culminating in a landmark 2003 book, Woodford developed a framework linking businesses' pricing decisions to inflation and monetary policy.

  • Hall — a Stanford professor who chaired the committee that dates U.S. recessions for 46 years — showed in a 1978 paper how consumers' spending decisions reflect expectations about future income.

Of note: The prize comes with an award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), up from 11 million kronor last year, to be divided between the two winners.

Flashback: Recent economics Nobels have recognized research on technological progress, economic prosperity and labor markets.

  • Last year's prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for their work explaining how innovation drives economic growth.
  • In 2024, Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won for their research on how institutions shape economic prosperity.
  • Harvard economist Claudia Goldin won in 2023 for research that advanced the world's understanding of women's labor market outcomes.

item.title: Judge halts Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads
item.description:
A federal judge on Sunday ordered the Trump administration to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump.

Why it matters: The ruling temporarily blocks the ads weeks before November's midterm elections as multiple lawsuits challenging the Trump administration's use of taxpayer money play out in court.

  • Sunday's ruling stems from a suit filed in the Southern District of New York by Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Common Cause, non-profit Democracy Forward and other plaintiffs.
  • A similar lawsuit, filed by the Democratic National Committee, was filed in D.C. federal court earlier this month.

The big picture: The Trump administration maintains that the ads are public service announcements and that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies.

  • Trump pledged to pay for the ads himself after both lawsuits were filed, though the White House told Axios there were no plans to reimburse the government for millions already spent on the ads.

Driving the news: The plaintiffs in the New York lawsuit allege that the Trump administration exceeded congressional authorization and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda.

  • In a brief order, U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found that a motion filed by the coalition was "not moot."
  • She found they had "demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," according to the order.
  • The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants.

What they're saying: The coalition said in a statement emailed by Democracy Forward it was "pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda."

  • The statement added, "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda."

The White House referred Axios to Trump's Truth Social post last week last week, in which he described the ads as a "positive promotion" for the U.S.

  • Representatives for the DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' Sunday evening request for comment.

What's next: A hearing is scheduled for Tuesday to discuss next steps in the case.

Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the plaintiffs and the White House's response to a request for comment.

item.title: Buttigieg gambles on a different path for 2028
item.description:
Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job.

  • That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year.

Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary.

  • Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path.
  • He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments.

Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state.

  • Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration.
  • Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate.
  • Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary.

Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week.

  • Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom.
  • In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract.
  • Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary.

Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver.

  • He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era.

What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios.

  • "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added.
  • Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass."

A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

item.title: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
item.description:
President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said.

  • The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next.

Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants.

Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries.

  • "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said.
  • "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready."

Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media.

What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote.

  • It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me."

State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices.

  • White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia.
  • "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said.

Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin.

  • A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests.
  • A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said.
  • On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

item.title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire
item.description:
President Trump claimed Sunday that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an "energy ceasefire" and will halt attacks on each other's energy facilities.

  • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky tells Axios the announcement "was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree."

Why it matters: An "energy ceasefire" would be a dramatic diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the winter. It remains unclear if Russia indeed agreed to stop the strikes.

  • Trump made a similar announcement last month, but neither party confirmed that there was a deal. Both Russia and Ukraine continued attacking energy infrastructure.

What they're saying: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • In a short interview after Trump's announcement, Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."

Catch up quick: The announcement follows days of escalating tensions between Trump and Zelensky over Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries.

  • On Friday, Trump announced a deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports in an effort to lower soaring fuel prices, infuriating Ukraine.
  • On Saturday, Trump called for Ukraine to replace Zelensky, accusing him of refusing opportunities to end the war.
  • Zelensky responded Sunday on ABC's "This Week," saying Ukraine would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. He also said Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

The big picture: The war with Iran has driven up global fuel prices, intensifying pressure on Trump to deliver relief for American consumers.

  • "It's more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others," Zelensky told ABC on Sunday.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.
