item.title: Republican midterm triage puts bleak outlook into focus
item.description:
Republican super PACs are flooding the airwaves in once-safe states, and pulling down ads for races that look like lost causes. President Trump, his approval ratings near record lows, is popping up in some of America's reddest states.

Why it matters: The polls showing Democrats headed toward a blue wave on Nov. 3 may not be quite right. But money — and how campaigns and PACs spend it — rarely lies. Nor do the contrails of Air Force One.

  • While Republicans are scrambling, Democrats are cutting some spending in contests they think are in the bag, such as North Carolina's Senate race.
  • No one wants to pay too much for a landslide, just as no one wants to throw good money after bad.

Republicans have been forced to pour well over $100 million into Ken Paxton's Senate race in Texas against Democrat James Talarico, and to plead for millions more to defend Senate seats in Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

  • Call it political triage. Republican operatives are making the kind of hard decisions that would be familiar to any battlefield medic: Save the wounded, and say a prayer for the lost.

Driving the news: Trump was in San Antonio on Wednesday to try to boost Paxton — his second trip in less than a week to Texas, a state he won by 14 points in 2024.

  • During the past week the president also has campaigned in Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska. He's planning another trip to Alabama this weekend for the Georgia-Alabama football game.
  • Vice President Vance showed up in Alaska this week, and will be in Ohio this weekend.

What they're saying: Republicans' efforts now appear more focused on calling for party loyalists to show up at the polls than on persuading new voters.

  • "Every time they up a buy [ads] on their end, it's always in the red states," said J.B. Poersch, president of Senate Majority PAC, the Democrats' main outside group working to win the Senate.
  • "Some of these outside [GOP] groups such as the Senate Leadership Fund and others are going to have to figure out where their money is best spent," said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost the GOP primary to Paxton.
  • "It looks like the money has already started to shift."

Zoom in: After pulling out of North Carolina (which Trump won by 3 points) last Friday, the SLF — Republicans' main Senate super PAC — put a fresh $14 million in normally deep-red Kansas.

  • This week, it sent a $5 million "insurance policy" to South Carolina (which Trump won by 18 points) to boost Republican Sen. Darline Graham.

The other side: Democrats are pulling down some advertising, but in states where polling has solidified in their favor. Their spending moves reflect confidence, not concern.

  • After the Senate Republicans' PAC cried uncle and pulled out of North Carolina, the Senate Democrats' group decided to go dark there as well.
  • One of Democratic group's ad reservations for North Carolina — which was actually in the Greenville market in South Carolina — was gobbled up by an allied group, Fresh Start SC PAC, which will use the time to attack Graham.

Between the lines: There's triage campaigning in House races as well, but it's not as pronounced — yet.

  • The GOP's Congressional Leadership Fund pulled down $1.1 million in advertising in Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, one of three GOP-held seats where former Vice President Harris won in 2024.
  • Democrats followed suit, with House Majority PAC canceling the $1.1 million it had reserved for the race. Both sides appear to agree that there's no obvious path for Republican Brinker Harding to win the seat left open by retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon.
  • In a San Diego-area House district, the Democratic group pulled down $200,000 in ads in a redistricted seat Harris would have won.

Zoom out: Republicans insist that their reallocation of funds doesn't mean they're admitting that the House or the Senate are lost.

  • One thing neither side disputes: The Senate Leadership Fund, which is closely associated with Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), is well capitalized.
  • That allows it to shore up candidates in red states, which wouldn't be necessary in a better political environment. In Texas, one of its subsidiaries spent $131 million in 17 days — more than $7.7 million a day.
  • The group has announced another $4 million for the Alaska race, bringing its total there to $21 million for Sen. Dan Sullivan, who's being challenged by former Rep. Mary Peltola.
  • In Maine, it has reserved another $8 million, for a total of $50 million for Sen. Susan Collins, who's in a battle with Democrat Troy Jackson.
  • In Michigan, it's putting in another $2 million, for a total of $53 million for former Rep. Mike Rogers in his race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
  • And in Ohio, it's spending another $14 million, bringing the total to $93 million for Sen. John Husted, who faces former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D).

What we're watching: All eyes are on Georgia. SLF announced an initial investment of $44 million there to back Republican Mike Collins, but Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has a healthy lead.

The bottom line: Republicans can dismiss bad polls as noise, or the result of liberal bias.

  • But their concern is evident in their thundering attack ads in red states such as Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

item.title: Exclusive: Mike Johnson raises record $156 million for House GOP
item.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson raised $30 million in the third quarter, bringing his total haul this cycle to $156 million as Republicans fight to hold on to their increasingly endangered majority, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Johnson's team says that's the most raised by a Republican speaker or leader at this point in an election cycle.

  • Johnson has distributed more than $91 million to Republican members, candidates, committees and state parties this cycle, according to figures first shared with Axios.
  • That includes $46 million transferred to the National Republican Congressional Committee, putting him on pace to make the largest cycle transfer to the group by a Republican speaker or leader.
  • He's also sent $21.5 million directly to GOP incumbents and $7 million to challengers.

Zoom out: Johnson's fundraising operation has brought in more than $220 million for House Republicans since he became speaker in October 2023.

  • That's a notable turnaround from when Johnson first took the gavel, when Republicans worried whether the relatively unknown Louisiana Republican could replace former Speaker Kevin McCarthy's formidable fundraising operation.
  • Johnson is also crisscrossing the country to help House Republicans, traveling to more than 40 districts across 22 states in the final stretch before Election Day, Axios previously reported.

What they're saying: "We are focused on getting unprecedented resources to the Districts that will decide the majority," Johnson said in a statement to Axios.

  • "With this continued momentum, we are in place to defy history and defend the House to save America from the far-left!"

House Speaker Mike Johnson raised $30 million in the third quarter, bringing his total haul this cycle to $156 million as Republicans fight to hold on to their increasingly endangered majority, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Johnson's team says that's the most raised by a Republican speaker or leader at this point in an election cycle.

  • Johnson has distributed more than $91 million to Republican members, candidates, committees and state parties this cycle, according to figures first shared with Axios.
  • That includes $46 million transferred to the National Republican Congressional Committee, putting him on pace to make the largest cycle transfer to the group by a Republican speaker or leader.
  • He's also sent $21.5 million directly to GOP incumbents and $7 million to challengers.

Zoom out: Johnson's fundraising operation has brought in more than $220 million for House Republicans since he became speaker in October 2023.

  • That's a notable turnaround from when Johnson first took the gavel, when Republicans worried whether the relatively unknown Louisiana Republican could replace former Speaker Kevin McCarthy's formidable fundraising operation.

item.title: Americans' trust in the food safety net is spoiling
item.description:
Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Americans' confidence in the safety of food on grocery store shelves — and in the federal government's ability to regulate it — has plummeted to new lows according to a new Gallup poll.

The big picture: Simultaneous illness outbreaks put federal regulators under a microscope earlier this year, as layoffs across the nation's health apparatus were already causing food safety angst.

By the numbers: Less than half of U.S. adults have a great deal (11%) or a fair amount (36%) of confidence in the federal government to ensure food safety, according to the poll, which was conducted last month.

  • On the flip side, a majority have not much or no confidence in the government's ability to police their food — a first in Gallup's trend, which has been intermittent for two decades.

Zoom out: Meanwhile, Americans' confidence in the food sold at grocery stores has mirrored that drop, falling to a record low of 65% saying they are somewhat or very confident.

  • That share has plunged from the 81% recorded in 2019.

Zoom in: That growing food safety suspicion is driven by Democrats and independents, while Republicans have actually become more confident in grocery store food.

  • The partisan chasm over the federal government's ability to ensure food safety has flipped — and widened — under the second Trump administration.
  • In 2024, half of Republicans had a great deal or fair amount of confidence in the government to ensure food safety, while nearly three-quarters of Democrats agreed.
  • By 2025, Democrats' confidence fell to 48%, and to 30% in 2026. Republicans, meanwhile, found new faith, with their confidence climbing from 62% in 2025 to 70% to 2026.

Catch up quick: This year's polling occurred during and after the federal government declared the end of an outbreak of Cyclospora, a parasite that caused stomach illnesses, two deaths and saw more than 500 hospitalizations across 21 states.

  • Federal health officials eventually traced the rapidly spreading surge to iceberg lettuce from supplier Taylor Farms.
  • But the food woes didn't stop there: This summer saw a flurry of overlapping recalls and FDA investigations, while health experts warned administration cuts had weakened the public health infrastructure responsible for detecting outbreaks.

Meanwhile, significant shares of Americans report concerns or strain about affording those groceries.

  • The food-at-home CPI, for grocery store or supermarket food purchases, was up 2.2% between August 2025 and 2026.

Friction point: That collides with an administration that's pushed whole foods as part of its "Make America Healthy Again" campaign under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

  • But Gallup's polling indicates Republicans have digested that food safety message far better than Democrats and independents.

Go deeper: America's next grocery shock is brewing

item.title: Military ordered to be ready for possible Iran strikes as Trump weighs timing
item.description:
The Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: The directive didn't include a specific date for launching strikes, and President Trump hasn't made any final decisions. But U.S. and Israeli sources say it could happen before the U.S. midterm elections and possibly the Israeli elections a week earlier.

The big picture: If major combat operations resume, they're expected to include massive bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets, sources say.

  • Resuming the war in the next three to four weeks could influence the midterm elections, in part because oil prices might rise in response.
  • "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told Axios.
  • A White House official said Trump has all options available at any time.
  • "The U.S. is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States."
  • The Atlantic reported earlier Wednesday that Trump is weighing striking Iran before the midterm election.

Driving the news: On Friday, Trump's national security team met at Camp David for several hours to discuss the war and other issues.

  • An Israeli official told Axios that part of the meeting focused on a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that it focused on "long-term" foreign policy planning.
  • Negotiations between the U.S. and Iran haven't made any progress. Qatari mediators are still waiting for an Iranian response to a U.S. counterproposal that included demands for nuclear concessions.
  • "The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out. After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly," a second Israeli official said.

Behind the scenes: President Trump spoke Wednesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was their second call in days, after barely speaking for many weeks.

  • A U.S. official said Trump and Netanyahu spoke about "remembrance and respect for the victims of the October 7 massacre."
  • The call took place after Netanyahu held a meeting with his national security team about Iran, the first Israeli official said.
  • Netanyahu spoke to Rubio on Monday.
  • If major combat operations resume, they will most likely be with the U.S. and Israel working in tandem and with the Israeli military participating.
  • The two Israeli officials said the Iranian regime is desperate and paranoid, which might lead it to strike first.
  • They said the Iranians have suffered two surprise attacks and don't want to experience a third.

Between the lines: Resumption of the war could also affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation.

  • A renewed escalation — or even a heightened state of tension or emergency — could benefit Netanyahu politically and prevent his opponents from attacking him in the final stretch of the campaign.

item.title: Student protest unrest spreads across Europe
item.description:
Police and protesters clashed in Liège, Belgium, on Wednesday as student anger over education costs and school conditions grew, echoing massive protests in neighboring France.

Why it matters: The protests are exposing broader anger across Europe over school funding and classroom conditions.

Catch up quick: Protests that began in Paris in mid-September as a localized demonstration by high school students have escalated into a massive nationwide movement, with students, parents and teachers' unions demanding more education funding.

  • There have been clashes between French police and protesters in recent days, culminating in a 15-year-old boy's hand being blown off by a police-fired stun grenade. More than 6,500 people — most of them minors —have been arrested since the protests began in France.
  • In Belgium, police have made at least 139 arrests in Liège since the protests began Oct. 1.

The big picture: The current wave erupted in France, but education grievances across Europe predate it, with crowded classrooms, teacher shortages, university cuts and soaring education costs fueling protests over government investment in education.

In Greece, students called nationwide school actions for Thursday, according to Euronews, including assemblies, walkouts, demonstrations and potentially occupations.

In Italy, high-school occupations began in Turin and Rome on Monday under the slogan "Let's do as in France."

  • Italian students cited underfunding, deteriorating school buildings and rising living costs among grievances they share with French students, and a delegation traveled to Paris in solidarity, ANSA reports.

In Ireland, thousands of university students demonstrated in Dublin earlier this month, demanding lower fees, more higher-education funding and affordable accommodation, per RTÉ.

In Germany, students, teachers, parents and unions rallied in September to demand greater education investment, more teachers and a more equitable school system, according to Tagesschau.

In Austria, student groups are preparing fresh demonstrations in mid-October after the country's university association warned of possible cuts of around €1 billion from the next three-year university budget, ORF reports.

Between the lines: The education unrest comes as several European governments face mounting pressure to rein in deficits while higher borrowing costs make their debts more expensive to service.

  • France and Belgium are each running budget deficits of more than 5% of their GDP this year, while Austria's is above 4%, according to European Commission forecasts.
  • That squeeze is forcing governments to make difficult choices over public spending.

The bottom line: The protests aren't one coordinated European movement, but students across several countries are mobilizing around their shared concerns.

Go deeper: The global fiscal reckoning is here

item.title: Trump's midterm strategists draw scrutiny over Russia-aligned work
item.description:
President Trump threatened Wednesday to fire two of his top political consultants if he finds a conflict, after reports that they advised a Russia-aligned government ahead of local elections there.

Why it matters: Chris LaCivita and James Blair are leading Republicans' midterm election strategy, putting their foreign consulting work in tension with their prominent roles in Trump's political operation.

What they're saying: Trump called the pair "outside consultants" in a Truth Social post Wednesday.

  • "They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients, but for that, you would have to ask them. They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C."
  • "I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there's a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!"

The other side: A source familiar with both consultants and the trip tells Axios that it was "a normal weekend full of calls and texts on the various races and our strategy/tactics in each."

Context: The nationalist party warned that new voting machines could threaten its hold on power, echoing Trump's repeated attacks on voting machines in the U.S.

  • A national election commission required the territory to use the new equipment.
  • The source said Blair and LaCivita were there for about 48 hours to give "strategic advice on Election Integrity and what to look for to spot and avoid potential election fraud, because it was the first election where Republic of Srbska was forced to use new ballots and Smartmatic voting equipment…which obviously made them nervous."

Between the lines: Caroline Wren, a registered lobbyist for Srpska, said the republic's abiding interest is in gaining stronger relations with Trump's administration.

  • "It's not about Russia. It's not about Putin. It's about Christians who want their freedom and autonomy," Wren said.
  • "The Trump Administration has made a huge priority of protecting and promoting Christians around the world and there is no better place to do that than the Pro-Trump Christians in the Republic of Sprska who have been demonized by the Europeans and Brussels for their Western values," she said.

Blair and LaCivita were "maybe on the ground for 36 hours," she said, observing that she saw Blair constantly on the phone discussing elections back in the U.S.

  • "Chris and James work around the clock to deliver wins for President Trump and Republicans here at home," she said.

Zoom in: Blair, who previously served as White House deputy chief of staff, left the administration earlier this year to work for MAGA Inc., a super PAC affiliated with the president.

  • He was also a senior adviser on Trump's 2024 campaign. LaCivita, the former co-manager of Trump's 2024 presidential campaign, is a senior adviser at MAGA Inc.

Catch up quick: LaCivita and Blair visited Republika Srpska, a semi-autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, ahead of local elections, according to the New York Times.

  • The two were reportedly recruited to advise the government on voting-related issues. They were hired to work for the government, not the nationalist party that controls it, though the party dominates the territory's government.

Yes, but: American political consultants have a long history of taking on foreign clients.

Zoom out: Trump's family businesses have expanded their foreign dealings since he returned to office.

  • The Trump Organization and its partners have more than 20 Trump-branded projects planned, under construction or opening abroad — more than triple the number of overseas properties operating before his return.
  • His administration accepted a luxury Boeing 747 from Qatar slated to eventually go to Trump's presidential library, while a UAE royal-linked firm bought a 49% stake in the Trump family's cryptocurrency business.
  • Donald Trump Jr. had his wedding bankrolled by a Putin-linked Russian oligarch and later repaid him after public outrage.

Go deeper: Trump's presidential profit machine bursts into the open

item.title: Syria considering sending troops to Yemen to fight Houthis
item.description:
Saudi Arabia and Syria are discussing sending Syrian troops to Yemen to join the counteroffensive against the Houthi rebels, three U.S. officials told Axios.

  • Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is seriously considering it, but he hasn't decided.

Why it matters: While the discussion is mostly between Saudi Arabia and Syria, the Trump administration has been consulted by both countries and is not opposed in principle to such a move, the U.S. officials said.

  • But sending Syrian troops could inject a religious dimension into the Yemen war and exacerbate the conflict. The troops could include Islamist Sunni foreign fighters who participated in the rebellion against the Bashar al-Assad regime. They would be fighting against the Houthis, who follow Zaydi Shiite Islam.

Driving the news: The Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a massive ground operation over the weekend against the Houthis. The offensive was designed to retake territories the Houthis control, including the capital Sanaa and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

  • A U.S. official said the issue of sending Syrian troops to Yemen came up during the meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and al-Sharaa in Riyadh earlier this week.
  • The Saudis want al-Sharaa to send troops in order to boost the Yemeni forces that are less trained than the Houthis.
  • While al-Sharaa hasn't signed off on the decision yet, the U.S. official said it is highly likely the Syrian president will accept the Saudi request.

Behind the scenes: The U.S. doesn't oppose sending Syrian troops to Yemen. It would provide more support for the Saudi-backed operation against the Houthis without the U.S. having to get deeply involved, a U.S. official said.

  • Trump administration officials also believe that deploying Syrian troops to Yemen would strengthen the relationship between two U.S. allies, Saudi Arabia and Syria.
  • Two U.S. officials said U.S. Central Command has been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed.
  • The White House and CENTCOM declined to comment. Spokespeople for the Saudi Embassy and the Syrian Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Zoom in: A source with knowledge of the discussions said the Syrian military could send 10,000–20,000 troops to Yemen.

  • The units under consideration are the 90th Division near Damascus and the 84th Division based in southern Syria near Sweida.
  • The 84th Division includes thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who came to Syria during the civil war to fight against the Assad regime under the umbrella of the HTS rebel group.

item.title: Exclusive: Inside Trump's AI science summit
item.description:
President Trump will attend a summit Thursday meant to empower scientists and position the U.S. as a leader in breakthroughs driven by "super intelligence," according to an announcement shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: The Trump administration is looking for industry to step in amid its cuts to government funding for science research and development.

Driving the news: The White House is announcing more than $1 billion in industry commitments for the Genesis Mission from AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and others.

  • The White House is also announcing a compute hub of more than 14 institutions across 10 southeast states, and a $1 billion investment in Georgia for student and faculty compute access.
  • The National Science Foundation and the Energy Department will invest more than $100 million in AI-driven science tools.
  • Leading scientists and "innovators" will attend the summit, the White House says.

Zoom in: The summit was inspired by a July report from White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios.

  • It highlights industry's increasing role in driving research and development, plus new mechanisms for funding and organizing research.

Catch up quick: Trump last November launched the Genesis Mission, which sets ambitious deadlines to accelerate scientific discovery.

  • In July, the White House announced that the effort would be expanded to more than 15 federal agencies.
  • Last week, the White House held another AI summit that focused on the rollout of America.gov, which aims to streamline government services using AI.

item.title: Microsoft looks to reboot the AI PC with Nvidia
item.description:
Microsoft on Wednesday unveiled a new class of Nvidia-powered Windows laptops, its latest effort to tie the operating system more closely to the AI boom.

Why it matters: Microsoft is trying to carve out a high-end laptop category for people who want to run demanding AI workloads locally, rather than rely entirely on the cloud.

Driving the news: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House AI official Sriram Krishnan were on hand in San Francisco as the company officially launched Microsoft Surface Ultra, a high-end laptop powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark chip that starts at $2,599.

  • "We have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang said.
  • Microsoft previewed the laptop back in June but left out key details around price and exact availability. It said at the time that Nvidia-powered devices would also be coming from the likes of Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, among others. Those devices, and the Surface Ultra, will be available starting Oct. 16.
  • On the software side, Microsoft unveiled a version of Copilot that can work using local models alongside those in the cloud, and the company also announced that Meta is bringing its Muse personal agent to Windows.

The big picture: Microsoft's first push into AI-powered Windows machines, known as Copilot+ PCs, got off to a rocky start after the delay of Recall, its signature feature.

Between the lines: Microsoft's pitch for on-device AI is that developers' appetite exceeds their companies' AI budgets, with the ideal being an approach that uses both frontier models in the cloud and local models when they can be effective.

  • "Hybrid intelligence exists because people's appetite for intelligence is effectively unlimited," Microsoft executive VP Pavan Davuluri said.
  • And before it even got to the hardware, Microsoft spent a fair bit of time outlining how it is making Windows more secure, ensuring that agents' actions are separated from those taken by humans and remain within preset limits.

item.title: Americans don't want taxpayer dollars funding campaign ads: poll
item.description:
Data: Reuters/Ipsos; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Nearly nine in 10 voters say using taxpayer money to pay for election-related ads featuring the president or Cabinet members is inappropriate, including 80% of Republicans, according to a recent Reuters-Ipsos poll.

Why it matters: The administration's decision to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on Trump-fronted ads weeks before the midterms is facing an uproar and overwhelming public opposition.

  • While the administration insisted the ads were actually PSAs, Trump later announced that a super PAC affiliated with him would foot the bill for future ads (but not reimburse the taxpayer dollars already spent).

Friction point: New polling suggests the TV spots, which the White House said "are a reminder for Americans to love their country," might not get much love from voters.

  • The poll of 4,506 adults found that just 9% of Americans find it appropriate to tap taxpayer funds for election-related television ads featuring the president or cabinet members.

Zoom out: A majority of Americans also panned other actions Trump has taken: 68% say it's inappropriate to block media outlets from entering the White House, and 72% say the same about naming federal institutions and buildings after a sitting president.

Data: Reuters/Ipsos; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Zoom in: A White House official contended in a statement to Axios that the "PSAs are clearly not political," saying Trump "is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action."

  • But one is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad, using the same footage and narration, with the campaign sponsorship tagline replaced with a disclaimer: "Paid for by the U.S. Government."
  • Earlier this month, Democrats called on the Government Accountability Office and the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate the use of taxpayer money to produce and air the ads.

Between the lines: Axios' Alex Isenstadt scooped late last month that the ads released so far were "just the beginning" and that Trump himself — pleased with the war-room-style social media posts his digital team regularly pumps out — was hand-picking the ads himself.

  • And it's not just the White House that's gotten in on promotional hype that blurs the lines with campaign content: The FBI's rapid response account released a video Tuesday applauding director Kash Patel — and criticizing Democrats, including Senate candidate Abdul-El Sayed.

The bottom line: As an election approaches where cost-of-living concerns are paramount, Americans have strong feelings about how their taxpayer dollars are spent.

Go deeper: "Love Me" artist doesn't love Trump using his song

item.title: Why France is a warning sign for the markets
item.description:
The good news about the epic shifts in global bond markets is that they mostly reflect economic fundamentals, not the kinds of panicky swings seen in a crisis.

  • The bad news is that there's a risk the disruptions metastasize into a broader crisis in an era of fractured politics across major democracies.

The big picture: Turmoil in the streets this week in France is the latest sign of hazards that await elected leaders who try to address yawning fiscal deficits head-on.

  • They are squeezed between voters who want to maintain public benefit levels and tax levels and a bond market that is resetting long-term interest rates higher — meaning that carrying on with wide deficits will come at a greater and greater cost to service debt.
  • That's why even what has been a relatively orderly repricing so far carries risks that are bigger than just high mortgage or corporate borrowing rates.

Driving the news: The relentless upward march of bond yields continued Wednesday morning. The French 10-year yield soared 0.18 percentage point, to 4.93%.

  • French yields are also surging relative to other countries that use the euro, especially Germany — the kind of fragmentation seen in the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s that originated in Greece.
  • But France is not alone. U.K. 10-year yields are up 0.12 point, to 5.49%, while the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is up 0.08 point Wednesday morning, reaching 5.36%, the highest since 2002.

Reality check: These are massive moves in markets that form the bedrock of global financial markets. And yet they don't appear to be driven by the kind of crisis dynamics and forced selling that fueled bond market volatility in the 2008 crisis, the 2014 Treasury flash crash and the March 2020 pandemic.

  • Rather, they've been driven by bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and deficit-running sovereign governments, exacerbated by surging energy prices that increase inflation risk.

What they're saying: "When you look at outright yield levels and/or spreads, a lot of this is still quite rational, and within the realm of what fair valuation should be, just given where nominal growth is and where we are in the cycle," Kunal Shah, the co-CEO of Goldman Sachs International, tells Axios.

  • "At this point, I still wouldn't say that we're anywhere close to the point of this being a broad financial stability risk or issue," says Shah, who is also co-head of fixed income, currency and commodities.
  • "What policymakers in Europe have shown us, though, is that when there's broader issues on contagion and/or disorderly functioning markets, that's when they can be quick to respond."
  • "Whilst the move in spreads has been very quick and sharp, in the broader context, we're still nowhere close to where we had got to in that previous European crisis," he says. "Financial conditions are tightening, but it's still not, I'd say, flashing red to the point that you need a backstop from the policymakers."

Yes, but: The European Central Bank has more powerful tools than it did in 2010 to address imbalances between European countries, and has shown willingness to use them. But it can't do much about the fundamentals of governments spending consistently far more than they raise in taxes.

  • And the global nature of the yield surge shows the common fiscal challenge across major economies.

State of play: In France, there have been violent clashes with police as teachers and students protest proposed wage freezes and school funding cuts.

  • In the U.K., a central political dispute is over the future of the "triple lock" pension adjustment mechanism, which all but guarantees pension costs will grow faster than the overall economy.
  • The U.S. Social Security trust fund is on track to be exhausted in 2032.
  • The rate adjustment of the last several weeks will increase already-onerous debt service costs for all advanced countries.

Of note: Those forces can create destabilizing effects for business even apart from the impact on rates. Shah, for example, says that U.K. governments lurching from budget to budget has made it hard for businesses making long-term decisions.

  • "I hope that at some point we'll be able to break out of this cycle, because it does stifle confidence and it just makes planning for the long term very hard," Shah says.

item.title: Raskin seeks to preserve Trump's D.C. "propaganda" in Smithsonian
item.description:
Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) introduced legislation Wednesday that would direct the Smithsonian to preserve and display artifacts he said reflect the rise of "governmental propaganda" under President Trump.

Why it matters: The bill will almost certainly fail in a Republican-controlled Congress. But it could preview how Democrats would scrutinize the president's use of taxpayer dollars to promote his image if they regain control in November.

  • Trump's drive to remake D.C.'s physical and cultural landscape in his image can be seen in banners bearing his face on government buildings and attempts to rebrand institutions with his name.
  • The administration also unveiled a plan last month to post warnings accusing Smithsonian leaders of pushing "personal, radical ideologies."

Driving the news: Raskin's bill directs the secretary of the Smithsonian to collect and display Trump's sprawling portraits hung outside of federal agencies at the Museum of American History.

  • It also calls for preserving signage or "artifacts" related to Trump's planned warning signs accusing the museum of "Ideological Capture."
  • The proposed new exhibit would also include narratives from Americans "who resisted and opposed the rise in authoritarianism."
  • It also calls for signage stating, in part, "Donald Trump ordered the installation of these signs without any Congressional authorization as required by the Constitution."

What they're saying: "Unlike President Trump's project of censoring, whitewashing and fictionalizing American history, my legislation will forever preserve his manifestations of authoritarian narcissism and his propagandistic assault on American history and American democracy," Raskin said in a statement.

  • The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Catch up quick: The Smithsonian has been caught in the crosshairs of the president's D.C. residency and his government-wide DEI purge that has targeted so-called "woke ideology."

  • Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced his retirement after more than three decades at the world's largest museum, education and research complex.

What's next: The Smithsonian's next leader will likely helm the institution through continued pressure under Trump — and through the fallout that follows.

Go deeper: Lonnie Bunch is leaving. The fight over the Smithsonian isn't

item.title: "The beginning of a new scientific paradigm": Zuckerberg's Biohub, U.S. and Google build virtual cell
item.description:
Mark Zuckerberg's Biohub is partnering with Google and the federal government in its ambitious effort to use AI for generating vast quantities of biological data that can predict how cells behave.

Why it matters: The ultimate goal is an AI model that lets scientists test potential experiments virtually, helping them identify the most promising ones before spending the time and money to perform them in the lab.

  • AI is capable of understanding proteins and other pieces of biology, but modeling an entire living cell is orders of magnitude more complex — and researchers don't yet have enough of the right data to do it.

Driving the news: Biohub, the Department of Energy, the National Institutes of Health, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, Meta and a collection of scientific organizations are collaborating to create and standardize data for what Biohub calls a "universal virtual cell."

The big picture: The goal is to use AI to explore many more scientific questions in biology virtually, allowing scientists to reserve expensive lab work for experiments most likely to teach them something important.

  • "If we can put more and more reasoning and intelligence into every single question that we actually ask in the lab, the value of those empirical results will be far greater," Biohub head of science Alex Rives told Axios.

Much of AI's recent progress has come from combining better algorithms, more computing power and enormous amounts of data.

  • Biology presents an additional challenge: Much of the information AI needs doesn't exist yet and has to be painstakingly measured from the physical world.
  • "We're at the beginning of a new scientific paradigm with AI," Rives said.

Yes, but: Biology is harder than many other AI domains because researchers need what Rives calls "empirical AI" — models that learn from biological evidence and can accurately predict what happens in the physical world.

  • "The big challenge in biology is to bridge that gap between compute and the digital world and the real physical world of biology and life," Rives said. "The way to do that is through data."
  • Such models could eventually help scientists investigate fundamental questions such as how aging and regeneration work — or medical questions such as which molecular mechanisms are responsible for Alzheimer's disease.

How it works: The first phase will create a broad map of cellular biology, gathering different kinds of information about cells and how they respond to changes.

  • Further out, Rives envisions models that could examine an individual's disease and predict its molecular causes and the best way to intervene.

The intrigue: The commercial partners will have one year of exclusive access to the data they develop before it is shared publicly.

  • Rives said the temporary advantage is intended to give companies a reason to contribute money while still ensuring the resulting data becomes an open scientific resource.
  • "We have to have some incentive for commercial players to be a part of this, and the embargo period creates that," Rives said. "But it's a one-year embargo. So what that means is that very rapidly, data becomes available broadly to scientific efforts."

Zoom in: The effort involves $1.8 billion in funding, data, computing and measurement technology.

  • DOE plans to invest more than $500 million over five years in biological measurement, modeling and computing, while NIH is bringing datasets and other resources resulting from more than $500 million in previous federal investment.
  • Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta are collectively investing another $300 million, while Biohub previously committed $500 million to the effort.

Flashback: When Biohub announced its initial $500 million effort in April, Rives told Axios one of the biggest unanswered questions was whether cellular biology would exhibit the same kind of "scaling laws" seen elsewhere in AI — with models becoming predictably better as they are trained on increasing amounts of data.

What we're watching: Rives thinks researchers won't have to wait particularly long to find out whether the bet is working.

  • Within a year of having the first large-scale dataset, he said, researchers should be able to train models, measure their capabilities and determine which kinds of additional biological data make them better.
  • "It's worked in every field, and it works in biology too," Rives said, pointing to AI's progress in protein biology.

item.title: America's changing disaster risk hits energy
item.description:
Hurricanes have long dominated efforts to make the power system more resilient to extreme weather. But America's energy buildout is running into growing risks from severe thunderstorms.

Why it matters: New energy infrastructure and data centers are being built in harm's way as severe weather risks shift, leaving more for developers and insurers to lose when storms hit.

Driving the news: Severe thunderstorms account for 40% of modeled global insured catastrophe risk, compared with 27% for hurricanes, according to analysis from risk analytics firm Verisk.

  • The U.S. accounts for $117 billion, or 68%, of Verisk's modeled global insured catastrophe losses.

Threat level: A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, potentially creating more favorable conditions for powerful thunderstorms. But the effects of climate change on severe storms are complicated.

  • National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration research scientist Harold Brooks told Axios that other atmospheric conditions needed for severe storms may become less favorable as the planet warms.

Reality check: Verisk's Jay Guin said growing exposure, more than climate change, is the dominant driver of rising insured losses, as more and increasingly valuable property is built in harm's way.

  • Guin says climate change contributes, but expanding development and higher reconstruction costs are much larger drivers.

Zoom in: America's changing energy system is creating new kinds of exposure.

  • Verisk is assessing risks to renewable projects in tornado- and hail-prone areas, where Guin said large hail can cause major damage to solar farms.
  • "While they are renewable, you have a new asset class that is quite vulnerable," he said.
  • Data center developers must balance natural-hazard exposure against access to land, power and water. Some sites have billions of dollars in property and hardware, raising the stakes for siting and engineering.

State of play: Tornado activity has increased about 10% in the mid-South while declining by roughly the same amount from the Texas Panhandle through western Kansas, Brooks said.

  • Population densities in rural areas of the Southeast are roughly 100 times those in the High Plains.
  • "It's 10 people per square kilometer in rural areas of northern Mississippi and Alabama, and so a tornado in that area can't miss buildings and can't miss people," Brooks says.

Zoom out: For infrastructure, Brooks said the biggest thunderstorm-related concern is flooding.

  • Heavy rain and flooding are "a huge threat to virtually all of our infrastructure," he said.

The bottom line: "There is no ... safe climate zone," Guin said.

item.title: Exclusive: Paxton privately blames campaign woes on Iran war, gas prices
item.description:
Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately lamented the impact of the Iran war and gas prices on his campaign in a meeting last month, telling a group of donors and lobbyists, "I don't make the decisions," according to audio obtained by Axios.

Why it matters: It's a candid admission from a close Trump ally about the challenging environment Republicans face this cycle.

  • Paxton, the Texas attorney general, was speaking to donors and lobbyists at a closed-door fundraiser in Washington, D.C. The audio was provided to Axios by a person, granted anonymity because it was a private event, who was in the meeting and is opposed to Paxton.
  • President Trump is set to rally with Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday.

Driving the news: Asked by one attendee what issues are "dragging" on his campaign, Paxton responded, "It's not tariffs. ... It's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," according to an audio file obtained by Axios.

  • "When it's over $6 per gallon for diesel ... people are feeling the pinch," he continued, adding that the rising cost of fuel "drives up food prices and everything else."
  • The Republican candidate said affordability is "by far our biggest problem" and "why we're having a hard time with numbers."

Paxton pointed to his tax cut plan — which includes new housing and health care write-offs and an expansion of the child tax credit — as his proposed remedy on affordability.

  • "I'm just trying to figure out ways I can help people. That's the only way: I can propose legislation," he said.
  • When an attendee posited that Paxton "can't stop the war," the candidate responded "right" and said he has "no control over gas prices."
  • "So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable. I don't make the decisions, and I don't ... know what's behind some of the decisions," he added.

What they're saying: "This is a non-story. The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store," a Paxton campaign person told Axios.

  • "President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families' pockets."

Between the lines: Paxton said in the same meeting that Trump's midterm convention in Dallas "dropped our numbers," and that control of the campaign is "all coming ... from D.C.," according to separate audio obtained by The New York Times and Politico.

State of play: Paxton is facing off with Democratic state Rep. James Talarico after unseating Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in a May primary runoff.

  • Polls of the race have largely shown Talarico narrowly leading. He would be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since the 1980s.
  • Paxton has for years been one of Trump's most loyal allies. Trump returned the favor in the primary by endorsing Paxton despite Senate Republicans' pleas for him to back Cornyn.

Listen to the audio:

Photo: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

item.title: 3 years later, Netanyahu faces reckoning over Oct. 7 in Israeli election
item.description:
Israel is marking the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 terror attacks three weeks before an election where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's personal culpability for the country's worst-ever security failure will be a central issue.

Why it matters: Netanyahu has never looked more politically vulnerable than in the weeks after Oct. 7, but he has defied expectations by keeping his government afloat — presiding over simultaneous wars and an atmosphere of perpetual emergency. Though the polls are tight, they leave a clear path for the ultimate political survivor to hang on yet again.

  • But Oct. 7 still looms over the country and his candidacy. The opposition lambasts him for refusing to take responsibility or allow an independent inquiry into the Hamas attacks that killed around 1,200 people.
  • Every other senior national security official who was in office at the time of the attacks has resigned, except Netanyahu.
  • Netanyahu's chief opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, lost his son and two nephews during the war in Gaza. Sources close to Eisenkot say he sees his main mission as replacing the man he holds responsible for allowing the Oct. 7 attacks.

Netanyahu blames the deep state.

  • His political and media allies — as well as his wife, Sara — have even spread conspiracy theories implying Israel was betrayed by its own security chiefs.
  • Netanyahu himself has claimed those security chiefs deliberately kept him in the dark and suggested he could have prevented the massacre if only they'd woken him up when early warning signs came in.

Driving the news: Recent reporting suggests Netanyahu had at least some warning.

  • Haaretz reported that United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed warned Netanyahu days before the attacks that Hamas was planning a major operation. Three sources with knowledge confirmed to Axios that UAE intelligence gave a general warning to its Israeli counterparts and that MBZ spoke to Netanyahu to make sure he received it. A former U.S. official said then-CIA Director Bill Burns was told several months later by MBZ that he had warned Netanyahu.
  • Other outlets including the New York Times also confirmed the story.
  • The Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal reported that Netanyahu received a similar warning ahead of Oct. 7 from Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel.
  • Netanyahu denied ever receiving warnings from the UAE or Egypt and sued several media outlets and journalists that reported he had.

Between the lines: While those stories have been widely discussed in Israel, the three violent years that have passed since Oct. 7 — the leveling of Gaza, the release of the hostages, the attacks on Hezbollah and two wars with Iran — have given Netanyahu ample opportunity to restore his reputation among many Israelis as a strong and decisive leader.

By the numbers: Most polls show Netanyahu's Likud party with 20-22 seats in the Knesset, down from 32, and his right-wing coalition with 50-54 — short of the 61 needed for a majority.

  • But the opposition is also unlikely to secure a majority without the support of Arab-Israeli parties, which are projected to win a combined 12-14 seats.
  • Polls reported by Netanyahu mouthpiece Channel 14 show the opposite, projecting the prime minister and his coalition winning a decisive 63-seat majority.
  • Seizing on the right-wing turn in Israeli society, Netanyahu has pressured his main opposition to rule out forming a coalition with the Arab-Israeli parties. That taboo could keep Eisenkot from taking power, though he could try to cobble together a minority government.
  • One possible scenario, if the polls prove accurate, is a hung parliament with Netanyahu staying on as a caretaker prime minister until another election is held.

The vote could determine not just Netanyahu's political survival, but his legal future as well.

  • Losing power would also mean losing any levers to delay or influence his ongoing corruption trial.
  • But if he wins, Netanyahu could argue he was acquitted by the people of Israel — and take stronger action to thwart the proceedings.

The intrigue: President Trump could give Netanyahu a boost by endorsing him, but so far he's declined.

  • Asked several times recently by Time magazine whether he supported Netanyahu, Trump dodged the question. He added, however, that he didn't believe the press reports that MBZ had warned Netanyahu.
  • Trump has privately blamed Netanyahu for the Oct. 7 failures, according to two people who have discussed the matter directly with the president. He's also mused about Netanyahu damaging Israel's international reputation.
  • However, Trump has stuck close to Netanyahu during the war in Iran and may still endorse him.

What to watch: Israel's election takes place a week before the U.S. midterms. If Democrats take back one or both houses of Congress, that will set up a battle over arms sales to Israel and even over the fate of $3.8 billion in annual military assistance.

  • The tenor of that debate may hinge in part on whether Netanyahu remains in power.

item.title: "Not safe for kids": Advocacy group urges OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT
item.description:
Common Sense Media is urging OpenAI to keep teens off ChatGPT, saying its new teen experience poses an "unacceptable risk" after extensive testing found shortcomings in safeguards meant to protect younger users.

Why it matters: OpenAI has made protecting younger users a central part of its effort to make ChatGPT safer, but the findings suggest some of those protections may give parents more confidence than they warrant.

  • "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice," an OpenAI spokesperson said.

Driving the news: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute said it tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds.

  • The group found ChatGPT generally did not provide instructions facilitating suicide or self-harm, eating disorders or sexual or romantic role-play, but said it was less reliable at recognizing when a teen needed outside help.
  • Common Sense Media said ChatGPT missed more than 1 in 4 instances in which its testers determined a crisis referral was warranted.
  • The group also said that on more than a dozen newly created, parent-linked accounts, testers could spend up to an hour discussing suicide, self-harm or disordered eating without triggering a parental alert.
  • Common Sense also found that Study Mode could be circumvented: Teens could choose "Show me the answer" and, during parent-set Study Hours, could easily bypass the rules.

OpenAI confirmed to Axios that the ability to exit Study Mode during Study Hours is intentional, not a loophole. The company said it designed Study Hours as a more flexible experience after consulting education experts and teens, rather than as a hard parental lock.

What they're saying: "ChatGPT is not safe for kids to use," Common Sense Media Youth AI Safety Institute head Tom Siegel told Axios.

  • Siegel said that what OpenAI announced in August still has the potential to be industry-leading, but gaps remain between what was promised and the current reality. "It feels much more of a marketing announcement that really was not backed up with the engineering work."

The other side: OpenAI says it has issues with Common Sense Media's methodology and findings.

  • OpenAI says much of Common Sense's testing of parental alerts occurred before the parent and teen accounts had finished linking, a process the company says can take several hours.
  • As for its age prediction system, OpenAI says it deliberately relies on multiple signals rather than simply accepting a user's stated age and can take up to two weeks to make a prediction. During that time, the company says users are given added content protections, though not as strong as the ones used in ChatGPT for Teens.
  • On crisis referrals, OpenAI says its larger-scale data shows an increase in hotline resources being displayed to under-18 users during the period studied.

Between the lines: Some of the disagreement reflects different ideas of what the safeguards are supposed to accomplish.

  • Common Sense treats the ability to exit Study Hours as evidence that the parental control is ineffective; OpenAI says that flexibility is deliberate.
  • Similarly, Common Sense's age test treats a user repeatedly identifying themselves as 13 without being moved into ChatGPT for Teens as a failure, while OpenAI says it intentionally requires multiple signals before making an age determination, while offering some strengthened protections during the time it is making its assessment.

The bottom line: Siegel says parents need to have strong conversations about AI and its risks with their teenage children and find other ways to make sure they are getting support, whether it be for homework or the challenges of life.

  • "We just can't outsource taking care of our kids to a tech product that is very early on and still quite buggy," he said.

item.title: "You suck": Emmer unloads on Senate Republicans
item.description:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is saying out loud what House Republicans have been grumbling about for much of the year: They're fed up with the Senate.

Why it matters You won't ever hear Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) or Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) talk about their Senate counterparts like this.

  • "There are no Democrats. There are no Republicans. They are just senators," Emmer told donors last week at a closed-door fundraiser Axios attended for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.).
  • Emmer said Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) "is doing the job that he thinks he's supposed to do. There's a certain fraternity sorority that is the U.S. Senate."

The intrigue: Emmer had a blunt message for senators who repeatedly say they can't pass House GOP priorities: "Don't just keep telling me 'Don't have the votes. Don't have the votes.' You suck."

  • Emmer said he once thought as a House member that he should stay out of the filibuster debate. Now, he thinks his colleagues should "get rid of the darn filibuster."
  • A Senate GOP aide retorted that what would "suck" would be losing the majority and that Republicans should be targeting Democrats instead of attacking their own side.

Driving the news: Emmer's comments are the most critical yet from a House GOP leader, but sum up the mood inside the conference.

  • More than a dozen Republicans paralyzed the House floor this summer in an effort to force Senate action on the SAVE America Act, the GOP's signature election bill that's become a major source of tension between the two chambers.
  • "We're frustrated with the Senate," Emmer told Axios in an interview after the fundraiser. "We feel like we've been doing everything we were hired to do, and a lot of it goes over to the Senate and it just sits there."
  • House Republicans put their votes "up on the board," Emmer argued, while senators "try to avoid" taking tough votes.

The big picture: House GOP leaders often say they've "done their job" when asked about unfinished business. But there's a clear implication in that phrase: The Senate hasn't.

  • Johnson has pointed to the backlog across the Capitol — including when he defended sending the House home early last month by noting that hundreds of House-passed bills were awaiting Senate action.
  • The speaker blames Democrats for that, but his complaints have put the spotlight on Senate GOP leadership.

Zoom in: Congressional Republicans spent much of the summer on completely different wavelengths over reconciliation 3.0, which doesn't require any Democratic votes.

  • Johnson pushed the Senate to take up the House's reconciliation framework, declaring in July that the Senate would pass it before leaving for August recess.
  • "That'd be news to me," Thune said at the time about Johnson's floated timeline. The Senate left town without any action on reconciliation 3.0.
  • "They can say all day long, you know, 'It's going to be hard.' Everything's hard. Give me a lecture about how hard things are. That's what I do every day. They've got to figure out a way to get it done," Scalise told Axios of his colleagues in the Senate in July.

The bottom line: Emmer stopped short of saying Senate Republicans have been a bigger obstacle to the GOP agenda than Democrats.

  • But he said two things frustrate lawmakers in the House when it comes to Senate Republicans: 1) They don't say what changes would get them to yes; and 2) they don't put themselves on the record when the answer is no.
  • "Put your money where your mouth is. Put your vote up on the board, and let's see where you really are," Emmer told Axios.

  • House Republicans put their votes "up on the board," Emmer argued, while senators "try to avoid" taking tough votes.

The big picture: House GOP leaders often say they've "done their job" when asked about unfinished business. But there's a clear implication in that phrase: The Senate hasn't.

  • Johnson has pointed to the backlog across the Capitol — including when he defended sending the House home early last month by noting that hundreds of House-passed bills were awaiting Senate action.
  • The speaker blames Democrats for that, but his complaints have put the spotlight on Senate GOP leadership.

Zoom in: Congressional Republicans spent much of the summer on completely different wavelengths over reconciliation 3.0, which doesn't require any Democratic votes.

  • Johnson pushed the Senate to take up the House's reconciliation framework, declaring in July that the Senate would pass it before leaving for August recess.
  • "That'd be news to me," Thune said at the time about Johnson's floated timeline. The Senate left town without any action on reconciliation 3.0.
  • "They can say all day long, you know, 'It's going to be hard.' Everything's hard. Give me a lecture about how hard things are. That's what I do every day. They've got to figure out a way to get it done," Scalise told Axios of his colleagues in the Senate in July.

The bottom line: Emmer stopped short of saying Senate Republicans have been a bigger obstacle to the GOP agenda than Democrats.

  • But he said two things frustrate lawmakers in the House when it comes to Senate Republicans: 1) They don't say what changes would get them to yes; and 2) they don't put themselves on the record when the answer is no.
  • "Put your money where your mouth is. Put your vote up on the board, and let's see where you really are," Emmer told Axios.
